metadata.methods_description: MEG was recorded in a magnetically shielded room with a 306-channel Elekta Neuromag Vector View system, sampled at 1 kHz with 0.03-330 Hz online filtering, across 8 task runs of about 10 min each. Head position was measured with HPI coils before each run, and EEG electrode, HPI and fiducial positions were digitized with a Polhemus system. EOG and ECG were recorded, and a resting-state recording followed the task. Individual T1 anatomical MRI was acquired on a Siemens 3T Prisma Fit scanner (1 mm slices, TR 2300 ms, TE 2.98 ms, flip angle 9°). Data were converted to BIDS with MNE-BIDS.

citation_details.venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
citation_details.abstract: In recent years, investigations into the psychological experience of time have rapidly accelerated. The experience of time could depend on a ticking internal clock or rely on contextual changes within and between events. Cognitive theories of memory propose that the presence of event boundaries, as defined by unexpected changes, is crucial for the segmentation of sequenced content and ultimately, the formation of long-term memories. Interestingly, the experience of change also influences the temporal distances between memories. Concurrent lines of research have developed similar theories on the experience of time, with salient contextual changes distorting temporal experience. citation_details.title: Supra second timing reflects oscillatory and aperiodic EEG dynamics
citation_details.author: Lorenzo Guarnieri, Ayelet N. Landau
citation_details.abstract: The perception of timing has been investigated across short and long timescales, with the latter usually underrepresented. Previous accounts of supra-second timing have often emphasised dedicated neural signals, yet whether timing performance over longer durations reflects specialised temporal mechanisms or domain-general neural excitability remains unclear. We examined this question in an interval reproduction task (2–4 s) using EEG, decomposing neural activity into oscillatory (alpha, theta) and aperiodic components and relating both to behavioural performance. At the neural level, separate analyses were performed on the interval encoding epoch and the following delay period. citation_details.title: An updated herpetofaunal species inventory of Iona National Park in southwestern Angola
citation_details.author: Javier Lobón‐Rovira, Pedro Vaz Pinto, François S. Becker, Krystal A. Tolley, John G. Measey, Bruce Bennet, Bastiaan Boon, Sango dos Anjos Carlos de Sá, Werner Conradie
citation_details.abstract: Angola has experienced an incredible increase of the knowledge of its herpetofauna over the past decade. However, accurate biodiversity inventories remain deficient for certain regions of particular conservation interest. We therefore provide an updated checklist of Iona National Park’s herpetofauna, with 75 recorded species, including five amphibians and 70 reptiles, 40 of these recorded for the first time in Iona National Park. These species comprise ~80% of the reptile diversity of Namibe Province. Therefore, this work recognises Iona National Park as the most reptile-diverse protected area in Angola and is potentially one of the richest in southern Africa. Consequently, this work enhances the importance of specific conservation plans in the area and the need for further investigation into the hidden biodiversity of this region.
